props.title: The Racket

sections.content: The Racket stands as a gritty film noir that captures post-war American cynicism through its unflinching look at police corruption and organized crime. Director John Cromwell, who previously helmed the noir classic Dead Reckoning (1947), brings a stark documentary-style approach that influenced later police procedurals. Robert Mitchum delivers a characteristically stoic performance as Captain McQuigg, an honest cop fighting both the mob and corrupt officials, while Robert Ryan burns with menacing intensity as racketeer Nick Scanlon. The film's themes of systemic corruption echo earlier noirs like Force of Evil (1948) while presaging later police dramas like The Big Heat (1953).

sections.content: The production history of The Racket reveals Howard Hughes' heavy-handed influence as producer, with multiple directors reportedly working on the film uncredited. This behind-the-scenes tension mirrors contemporaneous noir productions like The Big Steal (1949) and His Kind of Woman (1951), where Hughes' interference often resulted in multiple versions and reshoots. Despite this, the film maintains a coherent vision of urban corruption that builds on the 1928 silent film version and the original 1927 stage play.

The film's visual style, crafted by cinematographer George E. Diskant, employs stark lighting and cramped interior compositions that heighten the claustrophobic atmosphere. These techniques would influence later crime films like The Narrow Margin (1952) and Kansas City Confidential (1952), establishing a visual grammar for depicting institutional corruption. The night-time street scenes, with their rain-slicked streets and neon signs, became quintessential noir imagery. SUBHEAD: Impact on Police Procedural Genre

sections.content: The Racket helped establish conventions of the police procedural subgenre that would flourish throughout the 1950s. Its influence can be seen in films like Detective Story (1951) and Private Hell 36 (1954), which similarly explore the thin line between law enforcement and criminality. The film's emphasis on institutional corruption rather than individual moral failing marked a significant shift from earlier crime pictures.
